title: Reduce Unnecessary Body Bracing
learningGoals: Find one obvious layer of extra effort

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Reduce Unnecessary Body Bracing. You are ready to answer and notice a raised shoulder or gripping hand. Trying to relax everything becomes another demanding task.

We will find one obvious layer of extra effort, try a small comfortable adjustment, and speak without needing total relaxation. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Bracing means holding or tightening the body in preparation for something. Some effort belongs to movement and speaking. We are exploring an obvious added layer, such as a gripping hand, rather than diagnosing tension or searching for every possible tight muscle.

You may notice shoulders lifted, hands gripping or the jaw held while preparing to speak. We are not searching for every possible tension. Choose one obvious area and see whether you can use a little less effort there. You can speak before feeling completely relaxed, and a small adjustment is enough for an experiment.

Notice the distinction: A chosen adjustment is an experiment, not a total-body inspection or a condition for speaking. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: I want to ask about the plan. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. One chosen area of effort and whether the adjustment freed or crowded attention. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Notice one clear area of extra effort. Next: Make a small comfortable adjustment. Then: Say a useful short message while allowing ordinary movement.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: I want to ask about the plan. There are two possibilities. This part became easier over time. Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What must happen before you speak? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: One chosen area of effort and whether the adjustment freed or crowded attention. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: One chosen area of effort and whether the adjustment freed or crowded attention. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
